note: Historical and analytical content only. The atlas does not model eugenic policy or sterilisation as options. Figures are the commonly cited scholarly estimates; follow the sources for detail and debate.
intro: Eugenics was the idea that the state should improve a population's heredity by encouraging some people to have children and stopping others. Between about 1900 and 1945 it had support across the political spectrum and among scientists, doctors and reformers in Britain, the United States and much of Europe. In practice it meant segregating, sterilising and, in Nazi Germany, killing people judged unfit, most of them poor, disabled or from minorities. It was abandoned because the science was wrong, the methods were cruel, and the Nazi programme showed where it led.

uk.title: Galton coins 'eugenics'
uk.text: Francis Galton, Darwin's cousin, argued that talent was inherited and that the 'fit' should be encouraged to have more children (positive eugenics).

uk.title: Eugenics Education Society founded
uk.text: Later the Eugenics Society (now the Adelphi Genetics Forum). Members and supporters included figures across politics and science, from Fabian socialists to Conservatives.

uk.title: Royal Commission on the Care and Control of the Feeble-Minded
uk.text: Reported that 'mental deficiency' was largely hereditary and recommended state supervision, including segregation of 'defectives'.

uk.title: Mental Deficiency Act
uk.text: Created four categories of 'mental defective' (idiots, imbeciles, feeble-minded and 'moral defectives') and allowed their detention in colonies and institutions. 'Moral defective' was used against unmarried mothers and others judged deviant. Tens of thousands were held, some for decades. The bill passed with only a handful of MPs voting against; Josiah Wedgwood led the opposition. Sterilisation was left out.

uk.title: Wood Report
uk.text: Estimated that about 300,000 people in England and Wales were 'mentally defective' and argued for a 'social problem group', fuelling calls for sterilisation.

uk.title: Sterilisation bill defeated
uk.text: Major A. G. Church's Private Member's Bill to allow sterilisation of 'mental defectives' was refused leave in the Commons by 167 votes to 89.

uk.title: Brock Report
uk.text: A Departmental Committee recommended legalising voluntary sterilisation for people with 'mental defects' or certain inherited conditions. No government took it up. Opposition from the Catholic Church, Labour and trade unionists who saw it aimed at the working class, doubts about the science, and from 1933 the example of Germany, meant Britain never passed a sterilisation law.

uk.title: Mental Health Act 1959
uk.text: Repealed the Mental Deficiency Acts and ended the 'defective' categories. Long-stay hospitals continued; many institutions closed only in the 1980s and 1990s under care in the community.

abroad.scale: About 60,000 to 70,000 people sterilised under laws in 32 states
abroad.text: Indiana passed the first law in 1907. Buck v Bell (1927) upheld Virginia's law ('three generations of imbeciles are enough'). California carried out about a third of all US sterilisations. Coerced sterilisations of Black, Native American and Latina women continued into the 1970s, and in California prisons until 2010. North Carolina (2013), Virginia (2015) and California (2021) set up compensation schemes.

source.name: Wikipedia: Compulsory sterilization in the United States

abroad.scale: About 400,000 sterilised; about 70,000 killed in the T4 programme by August 1941 and 200,000 or more disabled people killed in total
abroad.text: The Law for the Prevention of Hereditarily Diseased Offspring (July 1933) set up 'hereditary health courts' that ordered sterilisation for conditions such as schizophrenia, epilepsy, deafness, blindness and alcoholism. Aktion T4 (from 1939) murdered disabled patients in gas chambers; its staff and methods were then used in the extermination camps of the Holocaust. Many victims were recognised and compensated only decades later.

source.name: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Eugenics

abroad.scale: About 63,000 sterilised, most of them women
abroad.text: Laws passed under Social Democratic governments as part of welfare-state planning. Many operations were formally 'voluntary' but were conditions for release from institutions, marriage or welfare. Exposed by journalists in 1997; the state paid compensation from 1999. Norway, Denmark and Finland had similar laws.
Alberta's Eugenics Board targeted Indigenous people, immigrants and women disproportionately. Leilani Muir won damages in 1996. Coerced sterilisation of Indigenous women was reported into the 2010s.

source.name: Wikipedia: Sexual Sterilization Act of Alberta

abroad.scale: About 16,500 sterilised without consent (about 25,000 in total)
abroad.text: The Eugenic Protection Law targeted people with disabilities and leprosy. In July 2024 the Supreme Court ruled it unconstitutional and ordered compensation.

abroad.scale: Hundreds of documented cases among Roma women
abroad.text: Roma women were sterilised without informed consent, at first under a policy to reduce the Roma birth rate. The Czech Republic passed a compensation law in 2021. The ECtHR found violations against Slovakia in V.C. v Slovakia (2011).

source.name: Wikipedia: Sterilisation of Romani women in Czechoslovakia

abroad.scale: About 270,000 women and 22,000 men sterilised, many without informed consent
abroad.text: A family planning programme under Alberto Fujimori, mostly in poor, Indigenous Quechua-speaking areas, run with quotas for health workers.

effects: No measurable effect on the conditions targeted. Most of them are not inherited in a simple way, many are not inherited at all, and recessive traits are carried by people who show no sign of them, so sterilising affected people barely changes their frequency.
Lasting harm to victims: loss of the chance to have children, trauma, institutionalisation and stigma. Compensation, where it came at all, came 50 to 70 years later.
Targets followed class, race, disability and sex rather than any biological measure. Women, poor people, minorities and Indigenous peoples were sterilised far more often.
In Germany it led directly to mass murder: the T4 killings were the testing ground for the gas chambers of the Holocaust.

abandoned.title: The science was wrong
abandoned.text: Genetics from the 1930s onward (Haldane, Penrose, Hogben and others) showed that most traits are polygenic and shaped by environment, and that the categories eugenicists used, such as 'feeble-mindedness', were social labels, not biological types. Lionel Penrose's Colchester survey (1938) undermined the hereditary account of learning disability in Britain.

abandoned.title: Nuremberg and human rights
abandoned.text: The Nuremberg medical trial (1946-47) and the Nuremberg Code made informed consent the foundation of medical ethics. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) and the ECHR (1950) recognised rights to bodily integrity, private life and to marry and found a family.

abandoned.title: Disability rights
abandoned.text: From the 1960s disabled people's movements, deinstitutionalisation and later the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (2006) made forced sterilisation a recognised rights violation.

abandoned.title: Exposure and redress
abandoned.text: Journalists and survivors exposed programmes in Sweden, the US, Canada, Japan and the Czech Republic, leading to apologies and compensation.

law_now.text: Sterilisation without informed consent is inhuman and degrading treatment: V.C. v Slovakia (2011), N.B. v Slovakia (2012), I.G. and others v Slovakia (2012).
Protect bodily integrity, private and family life, and the right to found a family.
Requires states to criminalise forced sterilisation. The UK ratified it in 2022.

law_now.law: Rome Statute, Article 7(1)(g); International Criminal Court Act 2001
law_now.text: Enforced sterilisation as part of a widespread or systematic attack on civilians is a crime against humanity, prosecutable in UK courts.
'Imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group' with intent to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group is genocide.

law_now.law: UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, Article 23
law_now.text: Disabled people, including children, have the right to retain their fertility on an equal basis with others.
Sterilisation of an adult who lacks capacity can happen only if the Court of Protection decides it is in that person's own best interests, never for social or eugenic reasons.

law_now.law: Offences Against the Person Act 1861 and criminal law of assault
law_now.text: Any surgery without valid consent or lawful authority is a serious assault.
